questions.q: What is the core idea behind "policy as code"?
options: Writing security rules only in a wiki page for engineers to read
Expressing a rule in an evaluatable language so it's enforced automatically and consistently, rather than relying on manual checklists
Replacing all container images with a single approved image
Disabling all automated scans in favor of manual review
questions.explain: Policy as code means a rule is written in a language that can be evaluated automatically every time, rather than depending on every engineer remembering and correctly applying a checklist.

questions.q: What is the relationship between Open Policy Agent (OPA) and Rego?
options: They are unrelated, competing tools
OPA is a general-purpose policy engine, and Rego is the language it evaluates policies in
Rego is a Kubernetes object; OPA is a Linux kernel module
OPA is deprecated in favor of Rego
questions.explain: OPA is the policy engine; Rego is the specific language used to write the rules that OPA (and tools built on it, like Gatekeeper) evaluate.

questions.q: What role does Gatekeeper play in a Kubernetes cluster?
options: It scans container images for vulnerabilities before they're pushed
It acts as an admission controller, evaluating resources against OPA policies and rejecting ones that violate them before they're scheduled
It manages secrets rotation for workload identities
It is a runtime security tool that watches live system calls
questions.explain: Gatekeeper applies OPA's policy model directly inside Kubernetes as an admission controller — it can reject a resource outright if it violates a defined policy, before that resource is ever scheduled.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate and a Constraint?
options: A ConstraintTemplate defines the reusable Rego rule once; a Constraint applies that template with specific parameters
They are two names for the exact same object
A Constraint defines the rule in Rego; a ConstraintTemplate applies it
ConstraintTemplates only work on Pods, while Constraints only work on Namespaces
questions.explain: The ConstraintTemplate contains the reusable Rego logic (for example, 'these labels must be present'), while a Constraint applies that same template with specific parameters, like requiring a particular label on Namespaces.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe policy as code as the "generalization underneath" Lessons 20 through 23?
options: Because it replaces every tool covered in those lessons with a single product
Because each of those lessons enforced a specific rule with a specific tool, and policy as code is the same underlying idea — write the rule once, evaluate it automatically — made explicit
Because those lessons have no relationship to policy as code at all
Because policy as code only applies to Kubernetes clusters, unlike those lessons
questions.explain: Image scanning, Pod Security Standards, required reviewers, and runtime rules were all specific applications of the same core pattern — writing a rule once and enforcing it automatically and consistently — which policy as code names directly.
